Vergilius was a man of great intellectual capacity, and was known for his ability to lead the discussion in the council of Salzburg. He also wrote a number of works of theology and various other religious treatises, such as: De gratia Dei (on the grace of God), De formatis sacramentorum (on the forms of sacraments), On the Holy Spirit (De spiritu Sancto), De principiis ecclesiae (On the principality of the Church), De ordinatione (On ordination), De doctrina Christiana (On Christian doctrine), De resurrectione Christiana (On the resurrection of Christians), and a work on the Eucharist.

Vergilius was in fact the first to use the term "Catholic Church" in the sense in which it is most often used today, namely as a synonym for the Church founded by Christ and represented by His Vicar, the Bishop of Rome.

Vergilius was buried in Salzburg Cathedral. His feast day is 9 November.

original: An exploration of the fundamental drivers behind long term shifts in the demand for, and supply of, land for agriculture, forestry and environmental uses over the next four decades. Topics include trends in food and bioenergy demand, crop productivity on existing and potential cro
sampled:
pland, urbanization and land cover change.

About this time last year, I was discussing the prospects for the crop insurance market in 2012. As you recall, I predicted that we were likely headed for another year of very large crop insurance losses, driven by the record-large 2011 crop insurance losses. While I was correct about the record-large losses, I was incorrect about the magnitude of the losses, as we have seen very modest levels of loss this year.

The current year’s crop insurance season is not quite finished, but it is safe to say that 2012 will go down as the least damaging year since 1974, and probably since 1960 as well. The most damage occurred in 2001, when $21 billion in losses were reported, but you will recall that 2001 was also a record-large crop insurance year. However, in many ways, this year’s crop insurance losses have been similar to what we have seen in 2002, 2006, 2009, and 2011. And those were the other three record-large crop insurance years, meaning that 2012 will go down as one of the lowest-loss years ever.

But while the headline numbers are down, the losses are not evenly distributed across all crop types. In 2012, the biggest losses occurred for soybeans, with a loss of $7 billion. The number is down from last year’s $7.4 billion in losses, but it is still a very significant amount of money.
